claims.text: For CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si, Mn, or Al, atomic size and redox potential govern whether oxidation produces a stable, coherent protective layer.
Atomic size and redox potential govern the initial stages of oxidation.
Redox potential becomes dominant over atomic size as oxidation proceeds.
The time-dependent dominance of redox potential causes composition inversion in the surface oxide.
Oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with the elements' interactions with the environment and are guided by thermodynamics.
The proposed mechanism applies to Si-, Mn-, and Al-containing members of the CrFeCoNiX family.
The applicable initial material state includes both single-phase and multiphase metallic solid solutions.
The applicable exposure range is 700–1000 °C in air or another oxygen-containing environment.
The proposed exposure-time boundary extends to 100 hours.
The mechanism predicts either formation of a stable, coherent protective oxide or formation of unstable oxides that crack or spall.
Traditional or non-high-entropy alloys provide the comparison baseline.
Mass gain, X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectrometry can be used to assess oxidation behavior and oxide structure.
Understanding of the atomic-scale oxidation mechanism in high-entropy alloys remains limited.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention specify exposure above 900 °C, whereas the stated conditions and boundary include temperatures from 700 °C upward. Thus, 700–900 °C is simultaneously included and outside the stated target regime.
